Mayor Mamdani and Chancellor Samuels Put Students First with Nation’s Broadest Generative AI Moratorium in Schools
September 2, 2026
Watch on YouTube
What you should know
Representing the most expansive student-facing AI policy in the country, the Mamdani administration prioritizes student safety and real, human instruction
NEW YORK –
Mayor Zohran Kwame Mamdani and Schools Chancellor Kamar H. Samuels today announced a moratorium on student-facing generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) use in schools, alongside a new screen time policy, a decision that will impact nearly 600,000 public school students, or two-thirds of the system’s total enrollment. The policy establishes a one-year moratorium, effective in the 2026-2027 school year, on student-facing generative AI for children in 2-K through 8th grade. It also introduces twice-yearly AI critical thinking modules for high schoolers, limited AI pilots for a small number of high school classrooms and age-appropriate screen time restrictions.
“Children need teachers and human connection in order to learn and grow. They need to develop skills alongside their peers, build relationships with educators and wrestle with tough problems on their own,” said
Mayor Mamdani
. “The tech industry wants us to believe that A.I.-powered early education is not only inevitable, but necessary. We do not see it that way. That’s why we’re implementing a moratorium on generative AI for students in 2-K through 8th grade and spending the next year studying the impacts of this technology.”
“We have a responsibility to ensure that rapidly-changing technology supports our children and their learning, rather than getting in the way of it,” said
Governor Kathy Hochul
. “New York State has been leading the way in our efforts to keep kids focused on learning and growing — not clicking and scrolling — and I commend Mayor Mamdani for building on this work and pushing our shared commitment to supporting New York’s kids forward.”
“As Chancellor and as a parent, I believe our job is to protect what makes learning work, while ensuring every child has the critical thinking skills they need before graduating,” said
Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels
.
“We’re putting guardrails in place to protect the human connection, curiosity and creativity that help children grow. We’re standing firmly in our belief that innovation does not mean more technology, and over the next year, we will lead with evidence to make sure technology serves learning — not the other way around.”
“As artificial intelligence rapidly expands into students’ lives, our city government has a responsibility to ensure this technology is serving, and not hurting, their development,” said
Public Advocate Jumaane D. Williams
. “This ban on student-facing AI for our youngest students, as well as age-appropriate screen time restrictions, are important steps in the right direction. Using this as a foundation but not a final word, we must continue to thoroughly review technologies that are entering the classroom and institute guardrails that promote the safety and well-being of New Yorkers.”
Representing the most expansive student-facing AI moratorium in the nation, the new policy eliminates AI use for students in grades 2-K through 8th grade. This includes all software that uses student-facing generative AI. Companion chatbots will be prohibited across all grades.
Throughout the 2026-27 school year, a new Technology in Schools Coalition, made up of students, educators, parent leaders, elected officials, advocates, union partners and experts in the field will convene to assess the impact of the moratorium and limited pilots. The coalition will publish a report with recommendations for future school years.
For a maximum of 50,000 high school students in general education classes, or approximately 5% of the public-school student body, five limited AI pilots will be introduced. All high school students will also have access to twice-yearly AI literacy classes designed to help them think critically about AI before they begin to rely on it.
The two 45-minute modules will introduce students to what AI is and is not, as well as AI-related bias, risks, ethical considerations and impacts on careers and future skills.
The limited pilots will be offered at a maximum of five classes per high school. All use will take place under the direct supervision of a trained educator and will involve carefully vetted AI tools. The pilots were selected based on rigorous safety and data privacy standards, their focus on teacher-guided instruction and their commitment to keeping students as the primary thinker in the classroom.
Pilot programs include:
Quill
: Accessed by English language arts classrooms, Quill is designed to support close reading, text analysis and the use of evidence to support claims. Students will use Quill for no more than 15 minutes per week.
Edia
: Accessed by math classrooms, Edia is designed to provide step-by-step coaching and prompt students to explain their reasoning. Students will use Edia for no more than 20 minutes per week.
Brisk Teaching
: Accessed through teacher-created activities, Brisk Teaching is designed to provide guided practice using teacher-selected texts or videos, with objectives and guardrails set by the teacher. Students will use Brisk Boost for 10 to 20 minutes once or twice per week.
Playlab
: To be used across multiple subjects, Playlab is designed to help students engage with assignment-specific applications and examine AI outputs for bias and reasoning. No more than two assignments per marking period will use Playlab.
Intel AI-Ready Schools
: To be used across multiple subjects, Intel AI-Ready Schools is designed to help students identify community problems and develop AI solutions through semester-long projects. Students will use the tool for one period per week.
Teachers will continue to be permitted to use AI for instructional planning and operational tasks, provided all tools comply with NYCPS safety standards. Exceptions to the policy will be granted for assistive technology usage by students with disabilities, multilingual learners and students participating in career readiness programs, like computer science.
With this new policy, students in 2nd grade and below will see restricted 1:1 screen time, with recommended caps of 30 minutes a day for students in 3rd grade through 5th grade and 45 minutes for students in 6th grade through 8th grade.
Under the new policy, all technology tools used in NYCPS will undergo an exhaustive review and will be barred if their functionality is ultimately determined not to be mission-critical to learning. The review will include vendor accountability for safety and transparency standards, ethics, evidence of learning design and instructional impact, prior research and the continuous collection of user feedback.
“Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Chancellor Kamar Samuels are taking a thoughtful and responsible approach to AI in our schools. Early-grade education must be rooted in building foundational skills through evidence-based practices, not experimenting on children with rapidly evolving technology. As Chair of the New York State Assembly Committee on Libraries and Education Technology, I introduced similar legislation, and I’m proud to serve on the advisory panel that will help New York City determine where AI can genuinely improve education while protecting students and preserving appropriate exceptions for children with disabilities,” said
Assemblymember Robert Carroll, Chair of the Assembly Committee on Libraries and Education Technology
.
“The AI policy set forth today protects the city’s youngest learners and prepares high school students to tackle the changing landscape they will graduate into. This policy is appropriately careful and responsive to community voices. I look forward to working closely with the Technology in Schools Coalition to further develop this policy and ensure accountability. As the coming wave of technology emerges, young people will be on the forefront — it will be their creativity, and ingenuity will lead the way. Our responsibility is to establish guardrails, such as these, to help them do it responsibly. This is a good step in that direction,” said
Councilwoman Rita Joseph, Higher Education Chair
.
“As a former middle school teacher, I'm so pleased to see that our Mayor is taking a nuanced approach to a new and rapidly changing educational tool. We took too long to respond to the effects of social media and smart phones on our youth. This combination of a 1-year ban with select pilot programs allows us to take a serious look at AI usage in schools and find a path that allows our students to adapt to our changing world in a safe manner,” said
State Senator Jabari Brisport
.
“This one-year ban on student-facing artificial intelligence technology use and restrictions on screen time through eighth grade are the right policies for optimal student learning and development,” said
Council Member Lincoln Restler
. “Credit to Mayor Mamdani and Chancellor Samuels for listening to students, parents, teachers and administrators and protecting our young people from the potentially harmful effects of untested technology. This pause alongside a commitment to meaningfully engage stakeholders in the months ahead will allow us to craft long term policies amid a rapidly changing technology landscape.”
“The announcement made by NYCPS detailing a whole new guidance on AI tools for students and teachers is a strong testament to parent and community organizing around protecting our kids,” said
Council Member Jennifer Gutiérrez, Chair for the Subcommittee on Early Childcare Education
. “AI is all around us, and while there are plenty of benefits to certain tools, there are also significant harms and we must foster the safest environments for our children. I am particularly encouraged by the greater accountability for tech vendors and the absence of student facing AI for our youngest scholars. I believe the Administration and NYCPS listened to parent and community concerns and I look forward to how this guidance will involve with the same principles.”
“We should never confuse a machine’s ability to produce an answer with a child’s ability to arrive at one. There is something sacred in the struggle to understand: the question asked twice, the page wrestled with, the mistake that becomes discovery, the teacher who sees possibility before a student sees it in themselves,” said
State Senator Robert Jackson
. “That is where intellect is formed and independence begins. In a democracy, we educate children not simply to know things, but to question, discern, imagine, and ultimately think for themselves. I commend Mayor Mamdani and Chancellor Samuels for recognizing that progress must earn its place in the classroom. Technology will continue to change, but our obligation must remain constant: childhood must never be the price we pay for innovation.”
“Tech companies have forced their way into every corner of kids' lives with big promises of benefits but little evidence to back them up. Enough is enough,” said
State Senator Andrew Gounardes
. “These new rules are an important step toward ensuring our kids' needs come before Big Tech's profits. By putting smart, thoughtful guardrails around the use of tech in schools, we can ensure learning comes first. Thanks to Mayor Mamdani and Chancellor Samuels for working to give our children the education they need and deserve.”
“AI is changing how we learn and work, and our kids need to be prepared to use it safely, think critically, and interrogate the information it produces,” said
Council Member Gale A. Brewer
. “I am encouraged that NYC Public Schools is taking a comprehensive approach, with age-appropriate AI literacy in K–8 and more focused instruction in high school, and I look forward to the program being shared with parents and staff. Thank you to Chancellor Kamar Samuels and Mayor Mamdani for preparing our students for a rapidly changing world.”
“The recent METR OpenAI report demonstrated how easily AI models can run amok, literally learning how to lie and cheat while covering their tracks to evade being caught deviating from their original code. Our ability to use generative AI with confidence that it won’t turn on our kids and do something else is tenuous at best. The policies announced today are well thought out, age-appropriate, and comprehensive — allowing for carefully chosen pilots for high schoolers and for those AI tools that provide access for students with disabilities and English language learners. Thank you, Mayor Mamdani and Chancellor Samuels, for pumping the brakes and creating this detailed policy,” said
Assemblymember Jo Anne Simon
.
“As a 14-year public school special education teacher and Chair of the City Council's Education Committee, I've seen how quickly new technology can outpace a school system's ability to manage it responsibly,” said
Council Member Eric Dinowitz
. “My committee's recent oversight hearing made clear the DOE needs a deliberate, evidence-based approach before AI tools reach classrooms unchecked. I applaud Chancellor Samuels' work on this policy and look forward to continuing our work together to ensure our students are kept safe and that technologies support and enhance learning.”
“AI and technology are central to New York’s economic future, as underscored by last week’s CBRE report showing that New York City now has more tech jobs than the Bay Area. We’re encouraged that high schoolers will have access to AI career readiness tools that can help prepare them for the workforce, and we recommend expanding this access beyond one hour per week in the future. At the same time, strong guardrails should enable age-appropriate learning that puts safety first, even at younger grades. Preparing youth for adult life and workplaces that rely on technology will require students to understand AI, question it, and use it safely, under the guidance of teachers. These are incredibly complex issues, and we give Mayor Mamdani and Chancellor Samuels credit for listening to all sides and creating a task force, which I am proud to serve on, to help shape what comes next,” said

.

passages: Generative AI is a type of AI that creates new text, images, audio, or other content in response to a user's instructions. These systems can produce inaccurate or biased information and can make it easier for students to bypass thinking they need to do themselves.
The student-facing restrictions described on this page apply specifically to generative AI.

For the 2026-27 school year, New York City Public Schools (NYCPS) is implementing a moratorium on student-facing generative artificial intelligence (AI) in grades 2K–8, with limited use in high schools, and screen time restrictions depending on grade.
Software that uses student-facing generative AI is not permitted in grades 2K–8.

Five pilots have been centrally approved for grades 9–12 (Quill, Edia, Brisk Teaching, Playlab, and Intel AI-Ready Schools). Any high school may apply for any of the five pilots, and each application will be reviewed on a case-by-case basis. Regarding individual student exposure to AI, we will ensure that students are participating in only one pilot.

Across all grades, this policy does not apply to assistive technology and associated screen time, provided through a student's Individualized Education Plan (IEP) or 504 Plan. Students with disabilities and English Language Learners (ELLs) will continue to have access to other necessary tools.

Teachers and other school staff members may continue using AI for instructional planning and operational tasks, subject to existing requirements, including the NYCPS Enterprise Request Management Application (ERMA) data privacy and security approval process, and NYCPS procurement rules. Additionally, AI may not be used for grading, behavior monitoring, or for placement, promotion, graduation, and other decisions about students. All special education documents are developed by qualified professionals; counseling, crisis intervention, and therapeutic support are provided only by qualified staff members.

The ERMA process currently reviews tools for data privacy and security. NYCPS is committed to building expanded evaluation capacity, including areas not covered by ERMA such as algorithmic bias, equity impact, and instructional effectiveness.

For AI tools being used in your child's school, contact your school principal. For concerns, you can contact your child's school, the School Leadership Team (SLT) or your Community Education Council (CEC).

While public feedback survey is now closed, you can share feedback directly to your school, participate in your school's PTA, attend your local Community Education Council events, or the Panel for Educational Policy.

The Technology in Schools Coalition, comprised of students, educators, parent leaders, elected officials, advocates, union partners, and experts in the field, will provide recommendations on the future of technology use in NYCPS classrooms and will deliver a report of policy recommendations in April 2027.
sources.limitation: Current NYCPS policy. Its ERMA description expressly limits the present review to privacy and security and says broader bias, equity and instructional-effectiveness evaluation capacity is still being built.

Guidance on
Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Screen Time
On this page...
A Note from Chancellor Samuels
As the largest school system in the nation, NYCPS is committed to leading the charge on key education issues, and that includes the use of technology in our classrooms. After deep analysis and engagement, we are enacting an artificial intelligence (AI) and screen time policy for the 2026–27 school year focused on protecting our youngest learners while also preparing our older students for a world shaped by AI.
We are putting safety first and ensuring technology serves learning.
Ultimately, as Chancellor and as an NYCPS parent, I believe that schools must be places where students think, read, write, reason, solve problems, talk with one another, and work through difficulty. They should also be deeply human places, where relationships with teachers and peers are central to learning;
we know that AI can never replicate the care, expertise, and commitment of our educators and staff
.
That's why we're putting guardrails in place to protect the critical human connection, curiosity, and creativity that help children grow. That's also why we are making sure every high school student learns how to use AI responsibly and safely, so they can navigate a workplace that is increasingly AI-driven.
We are putting safety first and ensuring technology serves learning—not the other way around.
To our staff members and families, I thank you for your partnership as we implement these guardrails. Our students are counting on us, and together we will provide the safe, engaged educational experience they deserve.
For the 2026–27 School Year
New York City Public Schools (NYCPS) is taking a cautious, developmentally appropriate approach to student-facing generative artificial intelligence (AI) and routine individual screen use. Younger students will have stronger limits. High school students will have limited, guided opportunities to learn about and use generative AI for specific approved purposes. This approach also reflects feedback we have received from families, educators, students, and other stakeholders, including through our spring 2026 public engagement process.
What Families Need to Know
Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Generative AI
Artificial intelligence is a broad term for computer systems that perform tasks such as finding patterns, making predictions, or creating content.
Generative AI is a type of AI that creates new text, images, audio, or other content in response to a user's instructions. These systems can produce inaccurate or biased information and can make it easier for students to bypass thinking they need to do themselves.
The student-facing restrictions described on this page apply specifically to generative AI.
AI and Screen Time Policy Updates
For the 2026-27 school year, New York City Public Schools (NYCPS) is implementing a moratorium on student-facing generative artificial intelligence (AI) in grades 2K–8, with limited use in high schools, and screen time restrictions depending on grade. The updated policies are as follows:

About Exceptions
Across all grades, this policy does not apply to assistive technology and associated screen time, provided through a student's Individualized Education Plan (IEP) or 504 Plan. Students with disabilities and English Language Learners (ELLs) will continue to have access to other necessary tools.
⤣
Exceptions to screen time limits include assistive technologies, assessments (e.g. screeners and diagnostics), out-of-school learning (e.g. remote instruction days), and centrally approved instruction (e.g. e-books, robotics, coding, simulations).
⤣
Grades 2K–8: Student-Facing AI Moratorium
Software that uses student-facing generative AI is not permitted in grades 2K–8.
Use of this technology in younger grades can interfere with human interaction and hands-on learning that we know is developmentally appropriate for children.
Grades 9–12: Student-Facing AI Limited, Guided Use
AI Literacy
All high school students will be required to complete two 45-minute AI literacy modules which will include lessons on how AI works, data privacy and bias, and appropriate uses of AI in school. Additionally, students pursuing career-readiness pathways such as CTE and certification programs, or participating in approved pilots will engage in a more in-depth AI literacy course. Schools will notify families when students participate in these approved programs.
Career Readiness
NYCPS offers career-readiness pathways, such as Career and Technical Education (CTE), FutureReadyNYC, and other certification programs. This coursework, along with other career-connected learning, may require use of certain AI tools to ensure students gain the career-specific skills needed to compete in the workforce. Students will only be allowed to use these tools with teacher supervision and in the context of career readiness.
Limited AI Pilots
Five pilots have been centrally approved for grades 9–12 (Quill, Edia, Brisk Teaching, Playlab, and Intel AI-Ready Schools). Any high school may apply for any of the five pilots, and each application will be reviewed on a case-by-case basis. Regarding individual student exposure to AI, we will ensure that students are participating in only one pilot.
NYCPS is developing a limited evaluation plan for the pilots. Tool selection was based on criteria such as:
Compliance approval with the NYCPS Enterprise Request Management Application (ERMA) data privacy and security review process.
Tools that support high school students with writing or math where the student does their own thinking.
Applications that teach teachers how to create and use their own student-facing AI tools based on the specific needs of their students.
Tools that directly enable project-based learning experiences for high school students.
Most of these tools are used for brief periods 1–2 times per week. Teachers are not replaced by such tools, rather the tool allows the teacher to design rigorous differentiated grade-level instruction delivered to students with a range of unique learning needs.
It allows teachers leading small group instruction to focus on one group at a time while providing the other students working independently a means of receiving support on their work that a worksheet cannot provide—teacher-assigned instructional tasks that are short in duration and engage students in productive struggle, self-paced learning and application of skills, and repetition and practice with feedback.

Screen Time Restrictions Across Grade Bands
1:1 student use of screens (direct interaction with a computer or tablet) in class should be used sparingly, with direct teacher supervision and for a clear instructional purpose.
The guidance is meant to reduce routine individual device use that interferes with teacher and peer interaction, reading and writing, discussion, hands-on learning, collaboration, and sustained attention.
The screen time policy is as follows:
Grades 2K–2: No 1:1 screen time
Grades 3–5: Recommend no more than 30 minutes of daily 1:1 screen time
Grades 6–8: Recommend no more than 45 minutes of daily 1:1 screen time
Teacher-led use of tools—such as computers, tablets, and interactive smart boards—is allowable for whole or small group instruction.
Accessibility Commitments
Every student has the right to a high-quality, inclusive learning experience in NYC Public Schools—including students with disabilities and multilingual/English language learners.

use. Devices and tools required for a student to meaningfully access instruction, participate in the classroom, and communicate with peers and teachers remain available under the policy.
Students with disabilities and English Language Learners (ELLs) will continue to have access to these and other necessary tools.
For Individualized Education Program (IEP) and 504 mandated technologies, NYCPS is legally required to provide those technologies regardless of our AI or screen time policies. There are also other accessibility tools used with students with disabilities and multilingual learners that provide important support outside of mandates, such as technologies that support communication.
The need for assistive technology and associated screen time is determined by the IEP or 504 team based on individual student needs.
How AI and Screen Time Policy Applies to Other Programs
Afterschool, Community Schools, and Contracted Early Childhood Education Programs
Any instruction by community-based organizations (CBOs) during school hours and in NYCPS buildings or contracted settings must abide by NYCPS AI and screen time policies. In addition to NYCPS's AI and screen time policies, contracted early childhood programs must adhere to technology use guidelines in the
Birth-to-Five policy handbook
. For afterschool, NYCPS will provide policy aligned guidance to providers. While the programs run under the oversight of the Department of Youth and Community Development or are operated by CBOs, and not NYCPS, we are committed to ensuring that students' experience during the school day and through extended learning/after school is aligned with youth development principles and grounded in relationship and skill development.
How Teachers and School Staff Members May Use AI
Teachers and other school staff members may continue using AI for instructional planning and operational tasks, subject to existing requirements, including the NYCPS Enterprise Request Management Application (ERMA) data privacy and security approval process, and NYCPS procurement rules. Additionally, AI may not be used for grading, behavior monitoring, or for placement, promotion, graduation, and other decisions about students. All special education documents are developed by qualified professionals; counseling, crisis intervention, and therapeutic support are provided only by qualified staff members.
Teachers remain responsible for the quality, accuracy, and appropriateness of what they produce. AI may assist educators, but it does not replace professional judgment.
How Software is Evaluated Before Reaching Your Child's School
Before any tool can be used with your child, it must be reviewed and approved. We call that review ERMA—the Enterprise Request Management Application. It's how we check that tools keep your child's data safe and protected.
The review is also how we keep the promises New York State law makes to you. Under New York State Education Law 2-d and its regulations, every vendor we work with must sign an agreement about how it will handle student information and provide NYCPS an explanation of what data it collects and how it protects it and meet recognized security standards. ERMA is where we confirm all of that.
The ERMA process currently reviews tools for data privacy and security. NYCPS is committed to building expanded evaluation capacity, including areas not covered by ERMA such as algorithmic bias, equity impact, and instructional effectiveness.
Learn more about the ERMA review process

NYCPS Ed Tech Portal
and logging in with their NYCPS credentials.

.
Our Commitments to You
These commitments define how NYCPS governs and uses AI in the service of students, families, and educators. We commit to:
Share Decision-Making
AI decisions are made through open evaluation and partnership. Families have a voice through Community Education Councils (CECs), Citywide Councils, the Panel for Educational Policy (PEP), and School Leadership Teams (SLTs).
NYCPS is forming the Technology in Schools Coalition to advise on the future of technology use in classrooms. Check back here for the launch of the coalition website and updates on progress during the school year.
Protect Student Data and Be Clear About AI
Student data belongs to students and families and is protected by law.
Empower Educators and Leaders
Educators are trusted professionals who receive the guidance and support needed to use technology responsibly, with professional judgment retained at all times.
Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)
Who do I contact to know about AI tools or raise concerns for my child?
For AI tools being used in your child's school, contact your school principal. For concerns, you can contact your child's school, the School Leadership Team (SLT) or your Community Education Council (CEC).
How can I give feedback on policies and technology in schools?
While public feedback survey is now closed, you can share feedback directly to your school, participate in your school's PTA, attend your local
Community Education Council
events, or the
Panel for Educational Policy
.
The Technology in Schools Coalition, comprised of students, educators, parent leaders, elected officials, advocates, union partners, and experts in the field, will provide recommendations on the future of technology use in NYCPS classrooms and will deliver a report of policy recommendations in April 2027.

Supporting Student Learning: NYCPS AI and Screen Time Policy for 2026–27
Dear Families:
As we prepare to welcome students back to school on September 10, I am writing to share details on
our 2026–2027 artificial intelligence (AI) and screen time policy
for NYC Public Schools (NYCPS).
This year, we are putting robust guardrails in place for student-facing AI and screen time, protecting the critical connection, curiosity, and creativity that help children grow. We believe our schools should be places where relationships with teachers and peers are central to learning. AI will never replace our teachers. It can never replicate the care, expertise, and commitment they bring to our schools.
To that end, for the 2026–27 school year,
we are implementing a moratorium on student-facing generative AI
(a type of AI that creates content in response to a user’s instructions)
in grades 2-K through 8
. This means that our early childhood, elementary, and middle school students will not be using AI tools as part of their learning.
We know that our older students are entering a world and workplace increasingly shaped by AI, and we need to responsibly prepare them for that world. So, in
grades 9 through 12
, student-facing AI will be
restricted to limited, carefully controlled high school pilots
that involve five vetted and approved AI programs. Students can also use AI under teacher supervision if participating in career readiness programs such as Career and Technical Education. Importantly, all high school students will complete AI literacy coursework to understand how AI works.
When it comes to student use of devices,
we are also setting developmentally appropriate limits on 1:1 screen time
(individual device use by children). Students in grades 2-K through 2 will have no 1:1 screen time. We recommend no more than 30 minutes of daily screen time for grades 3 through 5 and no more than 45 minutes daily for grades 6 through 8.
Across all grades, this policy does not apply to assistive technology and associated screen time provided through a student's Individualized Education Plan (IEP) or 504 Plan, and technology that supports language access per federal and State mandates for English Language Learners (ELLs). Students with disabilities and ELLs will continue to have access to necessary tools that provide important communication support.
Additionally, teachers may continue using NYCPS-approved AI tools for instructional planning and operational work, but AI may never be used for grading, behavior monitoring, or for placement, promotion, graduation, and other decisions about students. For more details and to read the full AI and screen time policy, please visit
schools.nyc.gov/AI
. This policy will apply for the 2026–27 school year. A Technology in Schools Coalition made up of students, educators, parent leaders, and other partners will help inform our policy for the 2027–28 school year.
Thank you in advance for your partnership. Implementing this policy successfully will require collaboration across the entire NYCPS community, and our students deserve nothing less.
Sincerely,
Kamar H. Samuels
Chancellor

Headline: NYC, the nation’s largest school system, bans AI for students through 8th grade
By Anthony Izaguirre
Published September 2, 2026.

NEW YORK (AP) — New York City’s public schools will temporarily ban elementary and middle school students from using generative artificial intelligence tools during the upcoming school year, Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced Wednesday.

The one-year moratorium — part of a broader assessment of how children in the nation’s largest school system interact with the technology — will apply to “all software that uses student-facing generative AI” for students through eighth grade, the mayor’s office said. It described the policy as the most expansive prohibition in the country.

At the same time, the city will establish twice-yearly AI literacy classes for all public high school students. It will also launch pilot programs allowing some high school students to use a handful of AI platforms under an educator’s supervision. Companion chatbots will be prohibited across all grades, officials said.

The approach comes as students, parents and schools across the country attempt to navigate the use of AI tools in the classroom and elsewhere. Schools are working to teach children how to incorporate the technology while preventing them from relying too heavily on it or using it to cheat.

In New York, the city will also recommend screen time limits for students, suggesting a daily cap of 30 minutes for students in grades three through five and 45 minutes for those in grades six through eight. Teachers will be allowed to use AI for instructional planning and operational tasks.

At least 37 states have official AI guidance that schools can use as a blueprint, though there is no single definition of AI literacy or consensus on how it should be taught. New York state last year approved a ban on students’ use of cellphones in schools.

City education officials will also conduct a broad review of all technology tools used in the school system and eliminate those deemed nonessential to learning.

Michael Mulgrew, president of the United Federation of Teachers in New York, praised the screen time limits but said the city’s AI policy “leaves many questions unanswered,” including how the Education Department “will be more aggressive in demanding the products it purchases have AI safeguards.”

Josh Golin, executive director of the children’s advocacy group Fairplay, said he would have preferred a longer moratorium and more time between the announcement and the start of the school year. “A year to evaluate is not nearly enough time,” he said, adding that the onus should be on AI platforms “to demonstrate that their products are effective at teaching kids, that they’re safe, that they’re not displacing face-to-face interaction and that they’re not leading to rampant cheating.”

New York City public school students are scheduled to return to classrooms next week.
